strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: extending score-based SBI (NPSE) to tall data settings without requiring MCMC or Langevin dynamics, which addresses a real limitation of the strongest existing baseline (F-NPSE of Geffner et al., 2023).
The derivation of the exact tall-data posterior score via backward transition kernels (Section 3.1) and the resulting Lemmas 3.1-3.2 are cleanly presented, with proofs provided in the appendix.

The two proposed variants (GAUSS with a constant covariance approximation, JAC with a Tweedie/Jacobian-based covariance) form a natural precision-vs-robustness trade-off, and the paper is honest that JAC is exact when score model error is zero but unstable when it is not.

Very thorough empirical evaluation: analytic toy models where the effect of controlled score error (epsilon) can be isolated, three SBI benchmark tasks plus six additional benchmark tasks in Appendix I, and a challenging neuroscience application (Jansen-Rit). The equivalent-time comparison protocol and multiple metrics (sliced Wasserstein, MMD) strengthen the evidence.

Good ablations and extensions: clipped variants, tamed ULA comparison (Appendix J), classifier-free guidance for learned prior scores, and partially factorized score models (Appendix K), showing awareness of alternative designs.

Code repository is provided, implementation details are extensive (Appendix E-F), and the limitations (e.g., MMD growing with n due to accumulated per-observation score errors) are explicitly discussed.
weaknesses: The Gaussian approximation of the backward kernels (Eq. 9-10) and the constant-covariance approximation behind GAUSS are heuristic; there is no theoretical control over the induced approximation error, only empirical evidence. Lemma 3.2's error term F is simply set to zero under assumptions that do not generally hold.

The MMD results (Appendix H.2, Figure 13) show increasing error as n grows for the benchmark tasks, which partially undercuts the claimed suitability for tall data; the paper attributes this to accumulation of per-observation score errors but offers no remedy beyond deferring to partial factorization.

The main empirical comparison is restricted to F-NPSE; baselines from the tall-data SBI literature (augmented NPE/NLE/NRE, hierarchical approaches) are not compared, so the scope of the 'superiority' claims is narrower than suggested in the abstract.

Some experimental reporting choices are questionable: discarding up to ~3% of the 25 ground-truth points as outliers (footnote 6) can favorably affect reported mean results, and the protocol should be more clearly justified.
GAUSS requires estimating Sigma_0 by running a 100-step DDIM per observation, adding a per-observation cost that is not fully accounted for in the runtime comparison against Langevin.

Writing has minor issues (e.g., typos, dense derivations in the main text), and the positive-definiteness condition on Lambda(theta) (Appendix B) is only given as a sufficient/intuitive condition, leaving the practical failure mode under-specified.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically relevant problem (amortized SBI with multiple i.i.d. observations) and the proposed GAUSS sampler is a sensible combination of existing ideas: the factorized score decomposition of F-NPSE (Geffner et al., 2023) with Tweedie-based second-order approximations of backward diffusion kernels (Boys et al., 2023; Song et al., 2023), replacing annealed Langevin dynamics with a DDIM-style chain.

The experimental study is extensive: controlled Gaussian/GMM toy models with analytic ground truth and controllable score error, three SBI benchmark tasks plus additional benchmarks in Appendix I, and a realistic neuroscience model (JRNMM), with sW and MMD metrics, multiple seeds, and an honest sensitivity analysis of Langevin step sizes (Appendix J).

The claim that the DDIM-style sampler is more numerically stable and computationally cheaper than annealed Langevin sampling is empirically supported in most settings, and the clipping/eta ablations add useful practical guidance.

The derivations (Lemmas 3.1 and 3.2, Appendix D analytical formulas) are, for the most part, coherent and reproducible from the manuscript, and the positive-definiteness discussion in Appendix B is a useful attempt to characterize when the approximation is valid.
weaknesses: Limited originality: the core ingredients (factorized tall-posterior score from F-NPSE, Tweedie second-order approximations from Boys et al. 2023, pseudoinverse-guidance-style Gaussian approximation from Song et al. 2023) are all pre-existing; the contribution is essentially a plug-in combination enabling DDIM sampling. The paper would benefit from a sharper articulation of what is genuinely new beyond recombination.

The central approximation is not theoretically justified: the correction term grad log L_lambda is approximated via Gaussian (Tweedie) surrogate backward kernels with no error bound, and Appendix B itself shows the positive-definiteness condition on Lambda can require the prior to be more concentrated than the posterior ('this does not make much sense'), i.e. the method's validity is not guaranteed even in the Gaussian case for realistic settings. No analysis of when/why the sampler remains usable despite this.

The headline claims of superiority are partially contradicted by the paper's own evidence: Appendix H.2 reports increasing MMD with n due to accumulation of approximation errors over the n score evaluations, and Figure 5 shows non-decreasing MMD for higher n. 'Superiority in terms of numerical stability and computational cost' (abstract) is therefore only conditionally true.

The baseline comparison is narrow and potentially unfair: only F-NPSE is compared, its code is unavailable (Appendix J admits a 'best-effort' reproduction), and Appendix J shows the ULA baseline is highly sensitive to step-size choices that the authors chose themselves. The claimed dismissal of NPE/NLE/NRE baselines relies on results from prior papers rather than a controlled comparison in this paper's setting.

JAC is largely a failed variant in practice: it diverges for n > 1 in all benchmark cases unless clipping is applied, a procedure the authors concede 'can introduce some bias'. Reporting JAC as a co-equal contribution overstates the results.

GAUSS carries an unadvertised overhead: a separate 100-step DDIM run per observation to estimate Sigma_0 is needed, which complicates the '5x fewer neural network evaluations' framing; the cost accounting should be presented more transparently.
Reproducibility gaps: the code repository link is empty in the manuscript (and footnote 13 is blank), preventing verification of the claims despite otherwise detailed implementation notes.

Presentation issues undermine polish: notation inconsistencies (v_t vs. upsilon_t vs. sigma_t, 'xi' vs 'zeta'), typos ('F-NSPE', 'consistenty', 'sensible' for 'sensitive'), a NaN row in Table 1 with no explanation, and duplicated text in Appendix K. There is no consolidated limitations discussion in the main text; key limitations (clipping bias, error accumulation, baseline reproduction) are scattered in appendices.

strengths: The core technical idea is sound and clearly derived: the paper shows how the diffused tall-data posterior score decomposes into known prior scores, individual posterior scores, and a correction term L_lambda, then approximates that term via Tweedie moment (second-order) approximations of the backward kernels (Lemmas 3.1-3.2, with proofs in Appendix A).

The proposed GAUSS sampler is genuinely useful for the field: it removes the need for annealed Langevin dynamics (the main practical drawback of F-NPSE) while reusing a score network trained on single observations, and it enables modern samplers like DDIM, as argued in Section 2.2 and the conclusion.

The empirical evaluation is broad and thoughtfully designed: two toy problems with analytic posteriors (including a controlled score-perturbation experiment quantifying robustness to score error epsilon), three SBI-benchmark tasks, additional benchmark tasks (Appendix I), and a challenging neuroscience model (JRNMM). Metrics (sW, MMD, MMD-to-Dirac) are appropriate and results are reported over many seeds/ground truths.

The paper is honest about failure modes: JAC diverging for n > 1 (Section 4.2), MMD increasing with n due to accumulated approximation errors (Appendix H.2), and limitations of Langevin sampling including a tamed-ULA variant comparison (Appendix J).

Implementation details are unusually complete (score architecture, training loss, normalization, MCMC ground-truth construction in Appendices E-F), supporting reproducibility, and a code repository is stated to be provided.
weaknesses: The key positive-definiteness assumption on Lambda(theta) (Lemma 3.1) is not verified in practice, and the authors' own analysis in Appendix D.1 (eqs. 28-30) concedes that the natural sufficient condition is nonsensical (it requires the prior to be more concentrated than the posterior). The method evidently works empirically, but the theoretical justification is left in an unsatisfying state and no empirical check or fallback when Lambda is not SPD is described.

The GAUSS algorithm has a hidden cost that weakens the computational claims: estimating Sigma_0 requires running a preliminary DDIM with ~100 steps per observation (Section 3.2/4). The '5x fewer NNE' and timing comparisons (Table 1, Table 2) do not clearly account for this pre-computation, which is only mentioned in passing.

The experimental comparison is narrow: only F-NPSE/Langevin is evaluated, justified by citing prior work, but amortized alternatives for tall/multiple-observation data (e.g., HNPE-style permutation-invariant NPE with set encoders) are directly relevant and absent. Given that GAUSS also accumulates errors with n (Appendix H.2), an amortized set-based NPE could be a strong competitor.

There is a selective-reporting concern: footnote 6 discards up to 3% of evaluation points (outliers defined via GAUSS's own 99% quantile or NaNs). This outlier-removal criterion is tied to one of the proposed methods and could mask instabilities that disadvantage baselines less favorably.

A significant portion of the machinery is imported rather than new: the Tweedie second-order approximations and the covariance formulas come from Boys et al. (2023) and Song et al. (2023); the contribution is the composition of these ingredients with the factorized tall-data score decomposition of Geffner et al. (2023). This is a legitimate contribution, but the originality is incremental.

The reported code repository link appears empty/unspecified in the manuscript, so reproducibility claims cannot be fully verified from the submission itself; also F-NPSE results are 'best-effort' reproductions (Appendix J) since the baseline code was unavailable, adding uncertainty to head-to-head comparisons.

Several presentation issues: no dedicated limitations section (limitations are scattered across appendices), duplicated sentences in Appendix K, notation inconsistencies (e.g., Eq. (6) summing s_psi(theta, x_i) with x undefined), and the claimed posterior in Eq. (1) convention (lambda^(1-n)) should be double-checked as it interacts with the (1-n) terms throughout.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important problem — sampling from the tall-data posterior in SBI without retraining or MCMC — and provides a clear, well-motivated solution built on a rigorous decomposition of the diffused tall posterior score (Eq. 7-8, Lemma 3.1-3.2), identifying the correction term missing from F-NPSE.

The two proposed approximations (GAUSS with constant covariance, JAC with score-Jacobian covariance) are well justified, and the trade-offs between them are analyzed honestly (JAC exact for analytic scores but unstable for learned ones; GAUSS robust).

The empirical evaluation is thorough and layered: controlled Gaussian/GMM toy models with analytic posteriors and injected score error allow precise diagnosis of robustness; three SBI benchmark tasks plus additional tasks in Appendix I with three metrics (sW, MMD, C2ST); and a challenging, non-identifiable neuroscience application (JRNMM) validated with the ℓ-C2ST diagnostic.

The paper is commendably honest about limitations: error accumulation with increasing n, failure of all methods on Two Moons and B-GLM (raw), scalability concerns of the Gaussian approximation, bias introduced by clipping, and the existence of Langevin settings that can work (Appendix K). The partially factorized extension (Appendix L.2) is a sensible mitigation.

Reproducibility is well supported: implementation details, training curves and model-selection strategy (Figures 5-6), and a code repository with pre-computed results are provided; the SPD condition on Λ(θ) is carefully analyzed in Appendix B.
weaknesses: The method is an approximation without theoretical guarantees: the Gaussian approximation of the backward kernels and the dropping of the F(θ, x1:n) term are justified only empirically; no error bounds or analysis of when the approximation degrades (e.g., as a function of n or posterior non-Gaussianity) is provided.

Claims of 'superiority' over F-NPSE rest on a best-effort reimplementation of the baseline (original code unavailable), and the baseline uses a fixed L=5 Langevin steps with τ=0.5; the authors themselves show in Appendix K that Langevin performance is highly step-size dependent, so the comparison may under-represent a carefully tuned Langevin sampler.

The empirical gains, while consistent, are modest in absolute terms on several benchmark tasks (e.g., SLCP where JAC-clip slightly beats GAUSS; GMM-uniform where the Langevin sampler is better), and JAC fails outright (diverges for n>1) in the learned-score setting, leaving effectively a single recommended algorithm.

Scalability to high n is limited: per-timestep evaluation of n score networks plus the linear solve introduces both cost and error accumulation, acknowledged but only partially mitigated via partial factorization which itself requires more simulations (×n_max) — weakening the tall-data motivation.

Minor presentation issues: the repository URL appears blank in the manuscript (pages 7 and 26), Bishop (2006) is cited but missing from the references, and Appendix L.2 contains a duplicated sentence.

strengths: The derivation of the exact score of the diffused tall data posterior (Section 3.1, Equation 7-8) is mathematically clean, and the identification of the missing L_lambda correction term as the reason Langevin steps are needed in F-NPSE is a genuinely useful insight.

The proposed estimators (GAUSS and JAC) are clearly presented as Algorithms 1 and 2, with proofs in Appendix A and a useful discussion of the positive-definiteness condition on Lambda(theta) in Appendix B.

The experimental protocol is unusually careful in the toy section: analytic ground-truth posteriors, controlled injection of score-estimation error (epsilon perturbation), and robustness analysis over dimension m, number of observations n, and error levels (Figure 7).

The paper is largely honest about limitations: it acknowledges error accumulation with n (Appendix H), the failure of all samplers on Two Moons and B-GLM (raw), and the bias introduced by the clipping procedure.

The application to the Jansen & Rit neural mass model with the l-C2ST diagnostic (Appendix J) demonstrates the method on a scientifically relevant, ill-posed inverse problem with non-identifiable parameters.
weaknesses: The contribution is incremental relative to Geffner et al. (2023): the core novelty is replacing annealed Langevin sampling with a DDIM-style backward chain using Tweedie-moment covariance approximations (already present in Boys et al., 2023), rather than a fundamentally new idea.

The baseline comparison is weak and potentially unfair. The only competitor is F-NPSE, reproduced as a best-effort because the original code is unavailable (Appendix K). No comparison to augmented NPE/NLE/NRE or HNPE is provided; the justification ('already shown to be inferior') relies on citations rather than this paper's own experiments, which is insufficient given the different sampling regime proposed here.

One of the two proposed methods (JAC) diverges in every benchmark task as soon as n > 1 (Section 4.2), which substantially undermines the claimed contribution; the practical method reduces to GAUSS alone, and the 'second order approximation' framing loses its main practical instance.

The computational cost claims are muddied by the GAUSS preprocessing: estimating Sigma_0,j requires running a 100-step DDIM per observation (Section 3.2), whose cost is not reported alongside the elapsed-time tables, and the 'equivalent time setting' gives GAUSS 1000 steps versus 400 for the baselines.

The removal of outliers defined as sW for GAUSS above the 99% quantile or NaN (footnote 4, Section 4.2) selectively filters failures of the proposed method; this is a questionable evaluation practice that inflates the apparent superiority of GAUSS.

MMD and C2ST results (Figures 12, 14) show increasing error with n, meaning the key claim of handling tall data well is only supported for moderate n and small parameter dimensions; all methods fail in several structured settings, weakening the significance claim.

There is no theoretical characterization of the approximation error introduced by the Gaussian approximation of L_lambda (only an informal intuition in Appendix C), despite the positive-definiteness condition on Lambda(theta) being assumed rather than verified in experiments.

Reproducibility is compromised in the submitted manuscript: the code repository URLs on pages 7 and 26 are blank, so the promised code and pre-computed results cannot be located. Typos ('proceedure', 'optimzer', 'installa­tion', a duplicated sentence in Appendix L.2) suggest insufficient polishing.
The writing oversells in places (e.g., 'demonstrate its superiority' in the abstract) relative to what the evidence shows, given the caveats above.

strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated and practically relevant problem (tall data SBI) and extends NPSE in a natural direction: constructing a direct DDIM backward sampler for the factorized tall posterior, removing the Langevin steps required by F-NPSE. The derivation (Section 3.1) identifying the correction term ∇log Lλ missing from the F-NPSE score is a genuine insight that explains when and why compositional score sampling needs correction.

The two proposed covariance approximations (GAUSS and JAC) are clearly distinguished, and the paper honestly reports that JAC is unstable with noisy scores while GAUSS is robust, which gives the reader actionable guidance.

The experimental design is thorough for a paper of this scope: analytic Gaussian and GMM toy problems with controlled score perturbation ε, three SBI benchmark tasks with multiple training set sizes and n values, additional benchmark tasks in Appendix I, a real neuroscience application with the ℓ-C2ST diagnostic, and ablations in the appendix (CFG prior score learning, partial factorization, tamed ULA comparison).
Reproducibility is good: code repository with pre-generated data, detailed implementation hyper-parameters, training curves, and explicit sampler settings.

Limitations are discussed honestly (error accumulation with n, failure on Two Moons and B-GLM raw, scalability of the Gaussian approximation), and the partially factorized extension in Appendix L.2 is a reasonable mitigation aligned with prior work.
weaknesses: The theoretical contribution is informal. Lemma 3.2 gives an exact decomposition only under zero covariance gradients, and the F(θ, x1:n) = 0 assumption is enforced by construction (stop-gradient) rather than justified; there is no analysis of the approximation error of the Gaussian kernel approximation (Eq. 9-10) or of how it interacts with the DDIM discretization. The positive-definiteness condition on Λ(θ) in Appendix B is discussed only at the level of a sufficient heuristic, so the sampler can in principle break down for some priors/scores.

The empirical claim of 'superiority' rests almost entirely on a single baseline, F-NPSE, which the authors had to re-implement without access to the original code (Appendix K). Given that the main advantage claimed is stability relative to Langevin sampling, a stronger or independent validation of the baseline (e.g., a well-tested public implementation) would be needed for the comparison to be fully convincing.

In practice only one of the two proposed variants works: JAC diverges for n > 1 in all benchmark settings and becomes unusable without the clipping heuristic, which is ad hoc, slows sampling, and is acknowledged to introduce bias. This weakens the contribution to essentially one algorithm (GAUSS) plus a failed variant.

Known failure modes are significant: MMD and C2ST degrade with increasing n (Appendix H), and all methods, including GAUSS, fail on multimodal or high-dimensional tasks (Two Moons, B-GLM raw). The main text's claim of 'superiority in sample quality for almost all examples' should be read against these acknowledged failures.

Some reporting choices raise concerns: outlier removal for GAUSS based on its own 99% quantile of sW (footnote 4) asymmetrically favors the proposed method, and the 'equivalent time setting' gives GAUSS 1000 steps versus 400 for the baseline, which complicates the fairness of the timing comparison.

Significance is moderate: the method is a sensible combination of existing tools (Tweedie moment projections of Boys et al. 2023, DDIM, F-NPSE factorization) applied to a specific SBI setting, and the scalability question raised in Section 4.2 remains open.
